title: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, CRANIOFACIAL ABNORMALITIES, AND SEIZURES
alt_titles: PSYCHOMOTOR RETARDATION, EPILEPSY, AND CRANIOFACIAL DYSMORPHISM

relationships.phenotype: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, CRANIOFACIAL ABNORMALITIES, AND SEIZURES

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures (NEDHCS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SNIP1 gene on chromosome 1p34.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures (NEDHCS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the SNIP1 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: Figure 3. Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia due to a homozygous SNIP1 mutation.
checks.explanation: The paper attributes the disorder (here called symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia) to a homozygous SNIP1 mutation.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 gene is located on chromosome 1p34.
checks.evidence_quote: Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia | 6 | 1 | rs2153337 | rs2225251 | 6.6 | 126
checks.explanation: The paper maps the locus to chromosome 1 but gives no band. 1p34 is standard gene-location nomenclature.

paragraphs.text: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures is an autosomal recessive disorder. Its main features are severe global developmental delay or psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, seizures, and craniofacial dysmorphism. It was first described in the Old Order Amish.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients were from Old Order Amish or Mennonite populations, received medical care at the Clinic for Special Children (CSC), and presented with a distinctive recessive clinical phenotype (Table 1).
checks.explanation: The disorder is described as recessive, and affected children are homozygous.

checks.claim: Severe global developmental delay or psychomotor retardation is a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected children have severe psychomotor delay and do not learn to walk or speak.
checks.explanation: Severe psychomotor delay is described.

checks.claim: Hypotonia is a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected neonates are hypotonic and feed poorly.
checks.explanation: Hypotonia is described.

checks.claim: Seizures are a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Multiple intractable seizure types can afflict an individual patient.
checks.explanation: Seizures and intractable epilepsy are central features.

checks.claim: Craniofacial dysmorphism is a main feature of neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures.
checks.evidence_quote: Dysmorphic features that evolve over time include a bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles, short hands, short tapered fingers, and broad thumbs
checks.explanation: Craniofacial dysmorphism and skull dysplasia are described.

checks.claim: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures was first described in the Old Order Amish.
checks.evidence_quote: Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia | A | – | Global developmental delay
checks.explanation: The disorder is presented as novel (no OMIM number) in the Amish (group A) and Old Order Amish controls were used, but the paper does not explicitly say it was first described in the Old Order Amish.

paragraphs.text: Puffenberger et al. (2012) studied Old Order Amish children with severe psychomotor retardation, hypotonia, epilepsy, and craniofacial dysmorphism. They used genetic mapping and exome sequencing to study this and several other new recessive disorders in Plain communities.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) studied Old Order Amish children with severe psychomotor retardation.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected children have severe psychomotor delay and do not learn to walk or speak.
checks.explanation: Severe psychomotor delay in Amish children is described.

checks.claim: The Old Order Amish children studied by Puffenberger et al. (2012) had hypotonia.
checks.evidence_quote: Affected neonates are hypotonic and feed poorly.
checks.explanation: Hypotonia is described.

checks.claim: The Old Order Amish children studied by Puffenberger et al. (2012) had epilepsy.
checks.evidence_quote: Multifocal spike-wave discharges from central, occipital, and temporal regions typically begin by 6 months of age and are accompanied by focal or generalized seizures
checks.explanation: Epilepsy is described.

checks.claim: The Old Order Amish children studied by Puffenberger et al. (2012) had craniofacial dysmorphism.
checks.evidence_quote: Dysmorphic features that evolve over time include a bulbous nose, wide mouth and tongue, broad jaw with protuberant angles, short hands, short tapered fingers, and broad thumbs
checks.explanation: Craniofacial dysmorphism is described.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) used genetic mapping and exome sequencing to study this disorder and several other new recessive disorders in Plain communities.
checks.evidence_quote: Among the Plain people, we have used single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) microarrays to genetically map recessive disorders to large autozygous haplotype blocks
checks.explanation: The paper combines genetic mapping and exome sequencing to study several recessive disorders in Plain communities.

paragraphs.text: Puffenberger et al. (2012) found homozygous mutations in affected children from Amish families, which is consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) found homozygous SNIP1 mutations in affected children from Amish families.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome data on three affected individuals from two sibships revealed 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region. Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly)
checks.explanation: Homozygous SNIP1 variant found in affected children from two Amish sibships.

checks.claim: The homozygous mutations in affected Amish children found by Puffenberger et al. (2012) are consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: Patients were from Old Order Amish or Mennonite populations, received medical care at the Clinic for Special Children (CSC), and presented with a distinctive recessive clinical phenotype (Table 1).
checks.explanation: The paper treats these as recessive disorders with homozygous variants.

paragraphs.text: In affected Old Order Amish children, Puffenberger et al. (2012) used homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing to identify a homozygous missense mutation in the SNIP1 gene (glu366-to-gly; E366G). The mutation segregated with the disorder.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) used homozygosity mapping and exome sequencing in affected Old Order Amish children.
checks.evidence_quote: Seven such conditions were selected for exome sequencing at the Broad Institute; all had been previously mapped at the CSC using low density SNP microarrays coupled with autozygosity and linkage analyses.
checks.explanation: Autozygosity mapping followed by exome sequencing was used.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) identified a homozygous missense mutation in the SNIP1 gene, E366G (glu366-to-gly), in affected Old Order Amish children.
checks.evidence_quote: Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly) (Table 3). PolyPhen-2 predicts the p.Glu366Gly substitution to be “probably damaging” (score = 0.99).
checks.explanation: Homozygous missense p.Glu366Gly in SNIP1 identified.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 E366G mutation segregated with the disorder in the Old Order Amish families.
checks.evidence_quote: In addition, siblings and parents were also sequenced, when available, to confirm appropriate segregation of the allele within the family.
checks.explanation: Segregation testing is described only in general terms for all disorders. No SNIP1-specific segregation data are given.

allelic_variants.name: SNIP1, GLU366GLY
allelic_variants.phenotype: Neurodevelopmental disorder with hypotonia, craniofacial abnormalities, and seizures

paragraphs.text: In Old Order Amish children with psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, and craniofacial dysmorphism, Puffenberger et al. (2012) identified a homozygous c.1097A-G transition in the SNIP1 gene, which results in a glu366-to-gly (E366G) substitution. Exome sequencing combined with homozygosity mapping identified the mutation.

checks.claim: Puffenberger et al. (2012) identified a homozygous c.1097A-G transition in the SNIP1 gene in Old Order Amish children with psychomotor retardation, epilepsy, and craniofacial dysmorphism.
checks.evidence_quote: Exome data on three affected individuals from two sibships revealed 34 homozygous variants in the mapped region. Of these, only one was novel, SNIP1 c.1097A>G (p.Glu366Gly)
checks.explanation: Homozygous c.1097A>G in SNIP1 found in affected Amish children.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 c.1097A-G transition results in a glu366-to-gly (E366G) substitution.
checks.evidence_quote: Symptomatic epilepsy and skull dysplasia | 3 | SNIP1 | c.1097A>G | p.Glu366Gly | 1.48% (6/406)
checks.explanation: c.1097A>G corresponds to p.Glu366Gly.

checks.claim: The SNIP1 c.1097A-G (E366G) mutation was identified by exome sequencing combined with homozygosity mapping.
checks.evidence_quote: Seven such conditions were selected for exome sequencing at the Broad Institute; all had been previously mapped at the CSC using low density SNP microarrays coupled with autozygosity and linkage analyses.
checks.explanation: Exome sequencing combined with prior autozygosity mapping identified the variant.
